list.listitem: Cyclospora cayetanensis is an uncommon cause of infectious diarrhea that should be considered in those with diarrhea during known outbreaks, who travel to endemic areas, or who are immunosuppressed with persistent diarrhea. C

Standard stool microscopy for ova and parasites has low sensitivity for detection of Cyclospora cayetanensis, which is better detected under microscopy with modified acid-fast staining, modified safranin staining, and/or autofluorescence or PCR testing where available. C
All patients with diarrhea found to be infected with Cyclospora should be provided supportive care and oral trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, which is considered first-line therapy. B

background.definition: Cyclosporiasis is a gastrointestinal disease caused by the protozoan parasite Cyclospora cayetanensis.

list.listitem: From 1997 to 2008, the overall population-adjusted incidence rates in the United States were 0.01 to 0.07 cases per 100,000 persons.
In 2015, the incidence of Cyclospora was reported to be 0.13 cases per 100,000 persons per year in the United States.

In the US, 370 cases of Cyclospora were reported via the Foodborne Disease Active Surveillance Network (FoodNet) from 1997 to 2009 with 56.2% occurring during June and July and 48.6% of cases associated with international travel.

In 2018, 2,299 cases of laboratory-confirmed cases were reported due to several fresh food outbreaks in the US in persons without international travel, which was much higher than the numbers of cases reported for the same period in 2016 (174) and 2017 (623).
The overall prevalence of cyclospora among humans worldwide is 3.55%
Cyclospora was found in 1.4% (3/221) of immunocompetent Polish patients with diarrhea returning from international travel to hot climates.
Cyclospora was found in 4.3% (13/300) of fecal samples of immunocompetent patients and 2% (6/300) of those that were immunocompromised with diarrhea in India.
Cyclospora was found via microscopy in 2.2% (12/544) of stool samples of persons living with HIV with acute (1/544) and chronic (11/544) diarrhea in Western India.
Cyclospora was found in 24% (88/366) of people living with HIV compared with 1.3% (3/200) of HIV-negative controls with diarrhea in India.
Cyclospora was found in 5% (2/38) of transplant patients with diarrhea in India.
Cyclospora is endemic in non-industrialized countries, where the majority of infections occur in children aged 2 to 10 years.
Cyclospora was found in 4% of patients with HIV/AIDS versus 1.8% in controls globally.
Cyclosporiasis is caused by ingestion of Cyclospora cayetanensis in fecally contaminated water or food, most commonly in tropical and subtropical regions internationally.
In the United States, 33.5% of cases from 1997 to 2008 occurred in persons with a documented history of international travel.
Outbreaks are more common during spring and summer in the United States and are more common in Eastern and Southeastern states.
Outbreaks of Cyclospora in the United States have typically been associated with imported fresh produce, such as basil, lettuce, cilantro, and raspberries.
Cyclospora is more common in persons living with HIV with CD4 counts <200 cells/μl.
Transmission occurs via the fecal-oral route, although excreted oocysts must mature under proper conditions into sporulates to become infectious, making direct person-to-person transmission unlikely.
Humans are the only known hosts for Cyclospora cayetanensis.
Cyclospora cayetanensis invades epithelial cells in the small intestine.
Screening for Cyclospora in asymptomatic individuals is not routinely recommended. C
Hand hygiene, food safety practices, and infection control measures reduce the spread of infectious diarrhea. B
There is no available vaccine for prevention of Cyclospora. C

For secondary prevention, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole prophylaxis with one double-strength 160 mg/800 mg tablet three times a week orally reduced recurrence in persons living with HIV who were previously treated for Cyclospora infection. B
Laboratory testing for Cyclospora should be considered in those with diarrhea during known outbreaks or travel to endemic areas. C
Stool microscopy detection of oocytes is improved with modified acid-fast staining, modified safranin staining, and autofluorescence. C
PCR testing for Cyclospora improves detection over traditional ova and parasite stool testing but at additional cost. C

Differential.Differential_Name: Causes of foodborne illness by pathogen:

list.listitem: Detection of Cyclospora organisms or DNA in stool, intestinal fluid/aspirate, or intestinal biopsy specimens.
The incubation period is typically 1 to 2 weeks.
Symptoms include watery stools, anorexia, weight loss, nausea, gas, abdominal cramps, and fatigue.
Symptoms may be more prolonged in those who are immunocompromised (e.g., persons living with HIV and low CD4 counts, and transplant recipients).
Fecal leukocyte examination and stool lactoferrin detection should not be used to evaluate acute infectious diarrhea.
Serum white blood cell count and differential does not clarify the etiology of diarrhea but might be useful clinically.

Cyclospora is not typically detected by routine microscopic stool examination for ova and parasites due to the small number of oocysts in stool, its small size, and inability to take up routine microscopic stains.

Stool microscopy for detection of oocytes may require at least 3 samples for adequate detection. Phase contrast microscopy can better detect spherical 8 to 10 µm diameter oocysts that have variable staining with modified acid-fast staining, red staining with modified safranin staining, and autofluorescence of the oocyst wall with UV lights. Cyclospora oocysts can be distinguished under microscopy from those of Cryptosporidium based on size. Both are seen using acid-fast stains, but Cyclospora oocytes have a diameter of 8 to 10 µm, compared with Cryptosporidium, which has a smaller diameter of 5 µm.

Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) analysis individually or in multiplex enteric pathogen PCR panels is an emerging diagnostic method with improved sensitivity but may not be available in all clinical laboratories.
Serological testing for cyclospora is not commercially available.
Endoscopy should be considered in immunocompromised persons with persistent diarrhea.
Small intestinal biopsy can show blunting of villi due to edema, infiltration of inflammatory cells, vascular dilation of the villous capillaries, and Cyclospora in vacuoles.
Oocysts can also be detected in small bowel biopsy samples.

People with acquired immune deficiency syndrome (AIDS) with persistent diarrhea should be tested for Cyclospora, in addition to Cryptosporidium, Cystoisospora, Microsporidia, Mycobacterium avium complex, and cytomegalovirus.

In solid-organ transplant recipents, the Infectious Diseases Community of Practice of the American Society of Transplantation recommends detection of cyclospora by stool microscopy using modified Ziehl-Neelsen or Safranin stains or autofluorescence or gastrointestinal multiplex molecular assays.
Most suspected cases of infectious diarrhea in the United States do not require diagnostic testing and can be provided supportive care.
Testing for Cyclospora should be considered in the setting of a possible diarrheal outbreak, regardless of the severity of diarrheal symptoms.
Stool examination for parasites should be considered in immunocompromised people with diarrhea.
Travelers with diarrhea of 14 days or more should be evaluated for Cyclospora.
All patients infected with Cyclospora should be provided supportive care, including rehydration. C
Oral trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole is considered first-line therapy. B
Oral ciprofloxacin or nitazoxanide are alternative treatment options. B

Infectious Diseases Society of America (IDSA) guidelines and CDC guidelines both recommend trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (TMP/SMX) double-strength 160 mg/800 mg orally twice a day for 7 to 10 days as the first-line treatment for Cyclospora infection. Longer treatment courses may be necessesary in persons with HIV.
Alternative treatments, with limited evidence of effectiveness, include ciprofloxacin 500 mg orally twice a day for 7 days or nitazoxanide 500 mg orally twice a day for 3 to 7 days.
Ciprofloxacin was found to be less effective than trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole in a small randomized controlled trial in treatment of Cyclospora in people living with HIV/AIDS.
Supportive care, including rehydration, is recommended by IDSA guidelines.
In solid-organ transplant patients, the Infectious Diseases Community of Practice of the American Society of Transplantation recommends reduction of immunosuppression if possible.
Consider referral to gastroenterology or infectious disease for recurrent cases of Cyclospora or if the specific etiology of persistent diarrhea is not found.
Consider hospitalization for those infected with Cyclospora who have severe dehydration.
Cyclospora infection may be self-limited in immunocompetent individuals; relapse can occur with re-exposure, particularly in endemic areas or those who are immunocompromised. B
Cyclospora infection resulted in a hospitalization rate of 6.5% and no deaths in the United States from 2000 to 2008, and a hospitalization rate of 4% with no deaths in the United States in 2015. B
Repeat stool testing is not recommended in most immunocompetent people with resolution of diarrhea. C
